analysis.one_liner: Bans hidden junk fees in hotels, tickets, and internet bills and requires airlines to seat kids next to parents for free.
analysis.headline: The Junk Fee Prevention Act never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required hotels and rental sites, ticket sellers, and internet, phone, and cable companies to show the full price up front, including mandatory fees, and to stop charging excessive or deceptive fees. It would also have banned most early-termination fees and required airlines to seat children 13 and under next to an accompanying adult at no extra charge, with refunds or rebooking if they could not. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers booking hotels or vacation rentals, buying event tickets, paying internet and phone bills, and flying with young children. They would see the true total price before buying, get refunds that include the fees they paid, and avoid surprise charges like family-seating fees and early-cancellation penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers buying lodging, tickets, phone service, flights

how_it_helps.text: Short-term lodging providers and ticket sellers would have to display the total price, including all mandatory fees, in every advertisement and at the first price shown, and that price could not change during checkout [S2] [S3].

The bill bans excessive or deceptive mandatory fees, requires ticket sellers to disclose refund policies and to warn buyers when they do not actually hold the ticket, and requires disclosure of how many tickets are available for sale [S2] [S3].

Internet, phone, mobile, and cable providers could not charge excessive or unreasonable early-termination fees, and the FCC would have to consider requiring disclosure of or banning other mandatory fees on those bills [S2] [S3].

Airlines could not charge a fee to seat a child 13 or younger next to an accompanying adult in the same class of service, and must offer rebooking or a full refund when adjacent seating is not available [S2] [S3].
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the fee rules, giving states power to sue for refunds and damages on behalf of residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ticket sellers, short-term lodging platforms and hotels, internet and mobile providers, and airlines, which collect billions in mandatory and add-on fees each year and would have to absorb compliance costs, reprice honestly, or drop fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline companies

drawbacks.text: The ban on 'excessive or deceptive' fees uses a flexible standard that regulators and courts would have to define, which could create compliance costs and litigation that businesses pass along in base prices [S3].

Banning early-termination fees removes a pricing tool providers use to offset the cost of subsidized devices or long contracts, which could lead to higher upfront prices or fewer promotional deals, though the bill carves out unreturned equipment and unpaid device costs [S3].

The family-seating requirement obliges airlines to hold adjacent seats without charging, which could complicate seat inventory in a business where airlines already sell specific seats for fees, and could produce more refunds and rebooking costs when seats are scarce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is straightforward: prices shown would be prices paid, and families would stop paying extra just to sit with their own children. The costs are mostly compliance and repricing burdens on companies, plus some uncertainty from the vague 'excessive fee' standard, which enforcement agencies would have to define over time. On balance the costs are modest and the consumer gains are broad and direct.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on March 22, 2023, for himself and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse [S3].
It drew two Democratic cosponsors in the Senate and no Republican ones [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; that was the only action of any kind for the life of the bill [S5].
The committee never held a markup or scheduled a vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline companies keep collecting mandatory and add-on fees, since the bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline fee collectors

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act and sought cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction; it was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Whitehouse'.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no positions were recorded beyond its two Democratic cosponsors and zero Republican cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill forces all-in pricing, disclosure of how many tickets exist, refund-policy disclosure, and warnings when a seller does not hold the ticket, cutting into fee revenue and speculative-selling practices that cost fans directly [S2] [S3].
Mandatory resort and cleaning fees would have to be shown in the first advertised price, ending the practice of quoting a low rate and adding fees at checkout [S2] [S3].
Excessive or unreasonable early-termination fees would be banned and the FCC would consider banning other mandatory fees that customers assume are included in the advertised price [S3].
Carriers could no longer charge for seating a child next to an accompanying adult and would owe refunds or free rebooking when they fail to, giving up family-seating fee revenue [S3].
